maintopic: SUPPORT PRICES-ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING SOYBEANS, LAMB AND WOOL
speechtext:
The Ontario soybean growers marketing board presented a brief to the agricultural stablization board in which they recommended that a support price of $2.50 per bushel be established on soybeans for the 1963 crop. In making this recommendation the marketing board expressed the wish for an incentive level of price support indicating that such would assist in diverting production from fall wheat and oats, that more protein supplement was needed for an expanding livestock industry, and that a reduction in soybean imports would be advantageous. They indicated that, were such an incentive price support level to be established, the marketing board would embark on a greater promotional campaign for expanded production.
Market returns for Canadian producers of soybeans in 1960 and 1961 were above the
[Mr. Hays.)
support levels. Higher prices in 1960-61 stemmed from a shortfall in world oil seed supplies. In 1961-62 they were maintained primarily by price support measures on a large scale undertaken by the United States government. In the current year the latter was also important, having the effect of encouraging producers to withhold supplies from the market. The demand for the limited quantities of oil seed meals available, however, with advances in soybean oil prices, resulted in rising soybean prices in spite of ample supplies statistically.
Canadian soybean prices, No. 1 or better, f.o.b. shipping points, rose from about $2.40 in August, 1962 to $2.57 during most of December. Up to the end of December 3.6 million bushels of soybeans had been marketed from a crop of about 6.6 million bushels. Prices jumped sharply in January and February and were in the neighbourhood of $2.75 per bushel. If the unmarketed soybeans indicated above are actually retained by producers, they will be in a position to increase their returns significantly by marketing during the remainder of the crop year. Prices are about 25 cents per bushel higher than about this time a year earlier. Producer returns from the 1962 crop should average between $2.40 and $2.50 per bushel delivered.
Based on the latest d.b.s. revisions of planted acreage statistics, current plantings are substantially below plantings of a few years ago. The recovery of soybean prices has not been of sufficient duration to improve acreage markedly. It would not be surprising, however, if a further recovery in planted acreage occurred in 1963.
It is considered by the board that the increased price in the market place should provide sufficient incentive for an orderly expansion of soybean production, and that a guaranteed price of $2.50 per bushel could bring undue optimism to the industry. Since the varieties of soybeans at present available have some limitations in terms of adaptability, it is felt that an incentive that would unduly expand the growing areas might ultimately be to the detriment of the individuals involved in such an expansion.
The board therefore recommends that the support price for soybeans be continued at 100 per cent of the base price for the 1963 crop, that is $2.15 per bushel for Canada grade No. 2 or better, 14 per cent moisture, delivered at elevator in Ontario. That is the answer to the question asked the other day.
Mr. Speaker, in answer to another question that was asked the other day I wish to inform the house that in so far as wool and lamb are concerned there will be the same

price of 60 cents a pound on wool and the same support price on lamb as last year.

speechtext:
wish to address a question to the Prime Minister. In view of the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce yesterday to the effect that there is no shortage of sugar supplies

in Canada at present and no shortage anticipated in the near future, would the Prime Minister tell the house what steps the government proposes to take to prevent profiteering at the expense of the Canadian consumer arising out of the increased price of this commodity?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO ACTION TO PREVENT PROFITEERING
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for having given me notice of his intention to ask this question. As my colleagues have already pointed out, the federal government is concerned with this matter in regard to any aspect of it which is covered by federal jurisdiction-combines, monopolies and actions in restraint of trade.
At present, as has been stated, there is no evidence that the high price of sugar in recent weeks has come about because of monopolistic practices or because of the action of a combine. The price of sugar in Canada, as has been pointed out, is high because the world price has gone up in recent months. In the last few days it has declined, and this decline will be very welcome to Canadian consumers. It must be recognized that the price is high because of a general world shortage of sugar.
As was pointed out yesterday by my hon. friend, there is no national shortage in Canada. Our stocks are at normal level. There is no need to expect any shortage in Canada. Our prices are high because they are linked to world market prices, and if world market prices now continue to decline from the high level recently reached, Canadian prices can be expected to decline as well.
Mr. Speaker, some have alleged that the prices are too high and that government action-that is, federal government action- should be taken to limit them. There is a constitutional aspect to this matter. I would point out that it is the provinces and not this parliament which have jurisdiction over prices in peace time, and if any law or regulation were to be made limiting prices it would have to be made by the provinces. If my hon. friends in this house feel that action of this kind is necessary in present circumstances to protect the consumer, their pleas, observations and requests on this matter should be addressed to the provincial governments, which alone would have the power to set limits on prices.

subtopic: REPORTED DANGER OF OUTBREAK OF ANTHRAX

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: REPORTED DANGER OF OUTBREAK OF ANTHRAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Horner) on May 28. His question was, what is the Department of Agriculture doing to prevent the spread of anthrax disease? His question was based on an article appearing in the Financial Post of May 25 this year which made reference to an outbreak in the Northwest Territories.
In July, 1962 an outbreak among buffalo in the Slave river area was uncovered. Measures to control and confine the disease were carried on jointly by the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. Veterinarians from the Department of Agriculture were dispatched to the area to conduct a survey and supervise the disposal of all buffalo carcasses. The Department of Agriculture established a quarantine area which prohibited the movement into or out of the area of all buffalo and parts of buffalo. The quarantine will remain in effect for this coming season at least. While no further cases have appeared, rigid surveillance of the area will be maintained.
More recently a case of anthrax was uncovered on a farm at Richmond, Fraser Valley,
Inquiries of the Ministry British Columbia, on May 4, 1963. Diagnosis of the disease was confirmed. The outbreak involved the loss of two cattle. Normal disposal, precautionary and quarantine measure were initiated, and no further cases have developed.

In order to uphold the rights of the French language, I suggest that alternately, in such circumstances, the statement be read in French or in English, and vice versa, so that it could not be said that one language has preference over the other.
I think that even in some other circumstances, it would be possible to proceed in the same manner without encroaching upon the rights of one language or the other. It seems to me this suggestion should receive the approval of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first of all I should like to apologize to the hon. member for Lapointe if copies of the resolution were not sent to him in both languages. I will try to see that this is done in the future.
The amounts of the appropriations requested in this resolution are intended to cover the amounts authorized by Governor General's warrants for the months of April
Interim Supply
and May and the amounts needed to provide for anticipated expenditures in the months of June and July. Broadly speaking, the government is asking for approximately four twelfths of the proposed expenditures for the year. In some cases the authority asked for is less than four twelfths, while in other cases it is more than that percentage. This is based on the time of year in which the proposed expenditures are normally made.
The bill that will be presented will be essentially in the same form as other interim supply bills submitted to the house on previous occasions. There will be a few changes which, of course, I will bring to the attention of the house when the bill is being discussed in detail. For the most part these changes are necessary because the expenditures for the months of April and May were authorized by Governor General's warrants.
Naturally, Mr. Chairman, I wish to assure hon. members that the passing of this interim supply bill will affect in no way the rights and privileges of hon. members to discuss or criticize any item in the estimates when it comes up for review in committee of supply. I should like also to add that it is the intention of this government to bring forward supply motions at an early date in order that the departmental estimates may be fully discussed.
I should like to mention also, Mr. Chairman, that the bill will include authority to borrow an additional amount of one billion five hundred million dollars if and when the necessity arises, for public works and general purposes. I shall be pleased to do my very best to answer any questions that may be raised by hon. members in connection with this resolution or later in connection with the bill.
The only other thing I think I should say at this time is that the request for interim supply at this stage of the session is, I believe, a customary one. I had thought of asking for only one month's interim supply plus the two months authorized by Governor General's warrants, but if I were to do this it would mean coming back to the house in June with a request for an additional month's supply. I was sorry to read in the press the other day that one of the senior civil servants of the government of Canada, the deputy minister of this department, is going to be relieved from the onerous load which he has carried for a good many years. I was rather intrigued the other night when listening to a television commentator speaking about these estimates, one of these wise boys who know all the answers. Those estimates, as we know, were based on substantially reduced estimates which we revised last summer. They were slashed very substantially following the foreign exchange crisis of last year, and the revised estimates which we prepared reduced the original ones by something over $200 million, I believe. When you look at the estimates and see that the statutory increases under health and welfare, for instance, amount to something like $100 million you can understand why I then wanted and again want now to express my appreciation to my then colleagues and the officials of treasury board for the way they co-operated in effecting a reduction in those estimates. I know there are some who thought it would be impossible to get the estimates down to the level we did, but I do not think we interfered in any way with the efficiency of the public service, and we did achieve a very substantial reduction which is now before us. We have heard a great deal about the economy of the country. I know the minister is probably looking forward to increased taxation revenue, though perhaps not increased rates of taxation, due to the expanding economy of the nation. The prime reason the economy is expanding, of course, is the fact that we have now and have had for the past year a realistically valued dollar. When the dollar was pegged at the level it now holds this accomplished a tremendous amount and was a tremendous service from the point of view of the economy of the country.
I will speak more about that in a moment. The exchange fund today is stronger than it

has ever been before. Dollars have been flowing in, and we are now in a very comfortable position so far as balances in the exchange fund are concerned. But as is obvious from the speech from the throne and certainly from private business plans thoughout the nation, if the government of Canada does not have to do so certainly Canadians generally and probably provincial and municipal governments will have to borrow very substantial amounts in the United States during the coming year which will result in a further flow of money into our country.
In this regard there is a very interesting situation developing. The United States rate is going up and our rate has been going down, and at the moment there is a very noticeable though not substantial reduction in the spread between the rate prevailing in the United States and the rate prevailing in Canada. If that situation should develop a little further, we may find it most difficult to attract additional moneys into Canada, because the encouragement which has heretofore been provided by the rate may not be as great as it has been in the past.
Therefore I think it behooves the government to watch its expenditures very carefully and to work toward a balanced budget. I know this cannot be done overnight. I know it cannot be done in one or two years, but we will have to attract money into this country and we will have to keep a firm, stable dollar at the present rate. I do not think that will be a very easy task if we continue to run substantial deficits. Instead of the deficits being reduced, as was our intention, they might very easily be increased, and as every hon. member knows-and no one knows it better than the minister-it is absolutely essential to maintain the present exchange rate and maintain a firm exchange balance.

I suspect there are very great pressures on other dollars than the Canadian dollar, as everyone knows who looks at the figures at all, and if that differential is not narrowed I think it might be very difficult always to get co-operation from the country to the south because it is having its own difficulties in that connection.

Even back in the days of 1867 and thereafter, when the C.P.R. was built it could only be built with government assistance at that time. We were struggling colonies; we merged, and Canada developed.
I think we have a unique record of public and private ownership. We are probably the only nation in the world with a great transcontinental railway system owned by the public and with, at the same time, another great transcontinental railway system operating in competition to it which is privately owned. We have a great publicly owned transcontinental radio and television system embracing this nation. We also have a series, and now a network, of privately owned stations. We have merged and combined in a unique way the benefits of public ownership and private enterprise. But essentially and fundamentally this has been and still is a

economic and budgetary points oi view, the country is presently experiencing a set-back, while it should be expanding. In fact, according to the estimates now before us, we see that we are going through a sharp recession, and I am going to explain why.

If we take a look at the total expenses provided for by the government, we notice that if an additional amount of a little more than $92 million is needed for interest during the current year, while last year the interest on the public debt amounted to $788 million, we shall have to pay $881 million this year.

I am very glad the hon. gentleman did, because I am going to suggest this: no one but a complete political ignoramus would have that view, and to send people out on this supposedly very critical, dangerous enterprise of riding herd on subversives in Canada, people who are complete ignoramuses, is to my mind disgraceful.
I have another case of a young man in my constituency, and I may say this house has not heard the last of this unless I get it cleared up. This young man enlisted in the navy. He came to the naval station in eastern Canada. He was in the navy for two months. He got excellent reports for his ability and his character. Then suddenly he was called in one day and told he was being released from the navy and being sent back home, with no explanation. He was assured there was no

Interim Supply
reflection on his character or his ability; the navy had just got tired of him and they were sending him home.
The boy had to go back to his home under this cloud, and when anybody asked him why he left the navy he had no explanation. His father wrote to me about it, and as soon as I saw the signature of the father I guessed what the trouble was. I wrote to the then associate minister of national defence in Ottawa, brought this case to his attention, and I told him I thought if he would investigate he would find it was a case of mistaken identity. I got a letter back from the associate minister saying it was thoroughly investigated and was not a case of mistaken identity.
I came to Ottawa last fall and again brought the matter up with the department. Again I got this unsatisfactory answer, and finally I was allowed to see this young man's file. The first document showed I had been quite right in my assumption that this was a case of mistaken identity.
This young lad had the same name as a man who had run against me as a communist candidate in 1953, and who lives in the same general area of Vancouver riding; but unfortunately for this highly intelligent intelligence service, I happened to know more about that communist candidate than they did, because his father had been in the same platoon as myself in the first world war, and I remember quite distinctly his marriage to a woman of Luxembourg, and the birth of their son. There was no connection whatsoever between these two families of the same name, yet this was the basis on which the highly intelligent intelligence service of this country sent this boy back from the navy, under a cloud that is still hanging over him.
Can you imagine what is going to happen to him when he applies for a job and is asked why he left the navy, and he replies they did not tell him and that he does not know? The implication right away is that there is something wrong with his moral character; and he has no means of refuting it.
Again this is a case of thorough incompetence on the part of those who are supposed to be protecting whatever secrets we are supposed to have in Canada, and I suggest the government will be well advised to have a complete overhaul of the operations of the R.C.M.P. in this regard. If the R.C.M.P. is to be entrusted with this sort of work, then it must recruit people of sufficiently average intelligence and sufficiently advanced educational qualifications so that their opinions will be of some value when they are submitted to others.
Right now the situation is nothing short of a disgrace, and I for one propose, in this one instance I have spoken of, not to allow this

young man to remain under a cloud for the rest of his life, or a considerable period of it at any rate, if there is anything I can do to expose the thorough incompetence, and I would say also, the complete lack of responsibility on the part of this supposedly intelligent intelligence service.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to be part of any designed delay in approving interim supply, such as the Liberal party opposition engaged in in the twenty fifth parliament, but for certain reasons I gave up my opportunity to speak in the throne speech debate, and I want to avail myself of this opportunity to make a few brief remarks. Since this is my first address to the twenty sixth parliament I would like to extend my congratulations to you sir, the deputy chairman of committees and to the Speaker of the house on your election to the offices you hold.
I have three observations to make and the first is completely non-contentious and concerns the conditions under which members of parliament are required to work. I am sure that if our constituents back home realized some of the difficulties under which we have to work, they would be most sympathetic. I am convinced from my own experience in working in the government that in most cases even a junior officer of some department is treated better than members of parliament. Our constituents would be surprised to know, for instance, that a member of parliament is not entitled to a private office, that he shares it with his stenographer and in many cases has to share it with another member and his stenographer. It almost seems that it is thought members of parliament act as such only while the house is in session. For example, we have no stenographic help between sessions. I for one-and I am sure most hon. members are in the same position-receive more correspondence on certain occasions outside of the sessions of the house than I receive when the house is sitting. We all know what long hours we are required to sit sometimes, particularly when the committee meetings start, and sometimes the only occasion we have to deal with our routine correspondence is Saturdays and Sundays. If we had, for instance, a dictating device it would be of great help to us and our stenographers.
Then, Mr. Chairman, I would refer to visits to our constituencies. We all agree that there is no substitute for personal contact with our constituents in order to know the problems which exist in the constituency. In many cases this is not, of course, a real problem, but I travel 3,000 miles to my riding and have to cross the straits of Georgia to get there. My train pass is of no value to me; it takes me eight days back and forth in the train. I am

supposed to visit my riding twice and I receive two tickets to enable me to do so. This is not right. I was very pleased to note that in the speech from the throne there was a reference to a committee on procedure. I hope the government will give these matters some consideration so that members of parliament may be better equipped to represent their constituents and to represent the interests of the parliament of Canada.
The second observation I wish to make, Mr. Chairman, concerns the general impression that is created in my mind by the speech from the throne which was concerned mainly, it seems to me, with a trend toward centralization of power and authority. Having had experience not only in the civil service but in other levels of government, I have clearly seen a continuing tendency, which is inherent in government, to centralize and to concentrate power at a higher level. To my mind this makes for less efficient service to the people of Canada. I know from personal experience that most civil servants are not only capable of greater responsibility but are anxious to take such additional responsibility. But I know that many civil servants have quit in disgust because they have to go to Ottawa to obtain approval for every little thing they do. This natural tendency exists anywhere, and I think it requires positive and conscious action by the government to reverse that tendency.
However, it seems to me that the present government is encouraging that tendency by its own actions. It seems to me the government is itself proliferating this tendency by creating more departments, more bureaux, more commissions, and even splitting departments. I think it is not insignificant that there was no particular reference in the speech from the throne or by any members of the cabinet to the Glassco commission on government organization. I had hoped that this government, as did the previous one, would have appointed one minister to be responsible for the over-all implementation of some of the recommendations of that commission. I wanted to make that observation, Mr. Chairman, and I for one will closely watch this trend. I think it requires positive action by the government to reverse it.
The third observation I wish to make, Mr. Chairman, is with regard to the economic condition of Canada. Hon. members can relax, because I am not going to quote a series of statistics; that has been done sufficiently in this house to date. I refer more particularly to tactics apparently being adopted by the government to deceive the people as to the economic conditions which existed at the time they took office. I think it is well to point out that at the time the
Interim Supply
Conservative government took office in 1957 and 1958 we were in a period of a descending level of economic activity, whereas when the Liberal government took office it was a period of ascending or accelerating economic activity. Yet this government adopted, by design it seems, the slogan that we must get Canada's economy rolling. I am amused by quite frequent references in the press to the fact that we in the House of Commons should stop reliving previous elections. I am not going to relive those elections but I want to make these points to show that some of the tactics the Liberals adopted in previous elections make them suspect. This is certainly the case with regard to their last slogan of getting the economy rolling. I refer first of all to the 1962 election. Other hon. members have referred to the revaluation and the pegging of the dollar. I was very pleased and interested to hear the Minister of Finance say, in answer to a question a day or two ago, that he had always advocated the revaluation and the pegging of the dollar. In 1962 the propaganda campaign carried on by the Liberals with regard to the revaluation of the dollar was, in my opinion, the biggest single factor which caused the reduction of the number of members of the Conservative party. The hon. member who is now representing Victoria, British Columbia, put out a pamphlet in which he said that our once sound dollar had been devalued. The reason I mention this point is to again remind the people that some of the slogans the Liberals are using today are suspect.
Then I come to last year's election, when the Liberals promised certain things which they now seem to have no intention of carrying out. I refer to a full page advertisement in the Victoria Daily Colonist of March 31, which is headed, "The policies of the Liberal party". This is apparently a complete run down of what they were going to do. One of the major items in this full page advertisement refers to health care. I will not take the time of this committee by reading the whole of that part of their advertisement, but any person who read it would automatically and logically assume that the Liberals would, as soon as they were elected, institute a health insurance plan. To date I have heard no suggestion from hon. members opposite that such will be done. Again I mention this because I think the people of Canada should be made aware that this current slogan of the Liberals, of getting the economy rolling, is false.
I am not going to quote statistics because statistics can be confusing to a great many people, as they often are to me. But I want to make two points to illustrate that in my

Interim Supply
riding, at any rate, economic conditions are at a very high level. For instance, the small fruits and cane fruits industry is the major industry in my riding. Last year the whole of the berry crop was sold before it was harvested, mainly because of the policies instituted by the Conservative government. This year the loganberry growers-and we have close to 300 of them-for instance, are concerned that they cannot meet the demands of the market. I quote one other factor in my riding, and that is the level of construction. In a riding such as mine, where there is very little industry and which is more or less a dormitory area, the level of construction is a good criterion of economic conditions. Nineteen sixty two was, I think, an almost record year of construction in my area. So far this year, in the first four calendar months of 1963 construction in the municipality of Saanich, which makes up the greater portion of my riding, has increased by close to 70 per cent over what it was in 1962. Certainly the people should be cautioned about the present tactics of the Liberal government, and the slogan which they use of "getting the economy rolling" should truly be to "keep the economy rolling."

In rising for the first time in this parliament to make some remarks, my first words will be to congratulate you, sir, on being elected to this important position as deputy chairman of committees. I would be pleased if you would convey my congratulations to the chairman of committees and to the Speaker. I also wish to congratulate the Minister of Finance on his appointment to the important portfolio he now holds. I am sorry the hon. gentleman is not in the house at the moment, but that is understandable; I know he will be right back. I hope he will read my congratulations to him in Hansard if he is not within earshot at the present time.
Having said that, I wish to bring to the attention of the committee, and I think this is the proper time to do so, the fact that we feel at this time, when we are starting not only a new session but a new parliament, great concern as to the efficiency of our organization. It is not enough to have excellent officials and officers of the house. It is not enough for the government to place legislation on the order paper. It is not even enough to extend hours of sitting and take measures of that sort if we neglect some other key considerations. I now wish to talk for a little while about a selection which has been made, presumably by the Prime Minister; a selection which I consider to be extremely unfortunate. I want it to be clearly understood that I approach this with no bitterness or
[Mr. Chatterton.J
malice and without making any reflection on the capabilities of the hon. gentleman concerned, especially as I number him among my friends. I consider him as one of my friends, at least within the limitations which the idio-syncracies of his character impose. I refer, of course, to the Secretary of State in his position as leader of the house. I think this is a very important position-a key position as far as the progress of the business of the house is concerned. I am not making any personal reflection on this hon. gentleman. As I have already said, he is a friend of mine. I recognize his great abilities. But I do feel that due mostly to the role he carried out in the last parliament, in an unofficial capacity, no doubt, on behalf of his party, he is completely unsuitable for the present position as leader of the house in which he is cast. I say he is a round peg in a square hole. He may be a very fine round peg, but he is in a completely square hole and completely unsuitable to his present position in the present state of affairs.
We had a situation at times during the last parliament when tension was high. It is possible that this situation may arise again. During the last five years this hon. gentleman has given over much of the ability of his very fertile mind to finding methods, admittedly completely within the rules, of slowing down and prolonging the conduct of the business of parliament. This is unfortunate in the light of what the responsibilities and duties of the leader of the house are. These duties are not very clearly defined, but there is a quotation which I may perhaps be allowed to read into the record. This is what Beauchesne has to say about some of the responsibilities of the house leader:
It is his task in the name of the government and the party in office to distribute over the session the program of legislation announced in the King's speech and to advocate it in the house. He assumes the duty of proposing all such motions concerning the agenda of the house as are deemed advisable by the government and is their spokesman in the debate thereon ... With regard to every development project, the leader is the final authority as to its general progress, as to the time to be given to its different stages and as to any application of the closure or other available method of shortening debate and bringing matters to a conclusion.
The quotation continues, but I shall not take up the time of the committee by reading further.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question about that question? Was that not in the days when the house leader, the real house leader, and who is still the real house leader, was always the prime minister? I think it was before the

time the humble functions I perform had been assigned to another member in this chamber.

I see some improvement in the hon. member already. He is expressing some modesty which, on other occasions, was not his custom. But as I understand it, and I may be wrong, the leader of the house does not entirely appropriate all of the responsibilities of the Prime Minister, although some of them he does; these particular responsibilities of the Prime Minister are delegated to the leader of the house.
I make these remarks only as a caution to the Prime Minister. I recognize from the start that it is a caution which will probably not be heeded. I doubt that any attention will be paid to it whatever. Yet I consider it my duty, because of a feeling of moral obligation, to point this situation out to the Prime Minister.
Many members of the opposition, maybe in all three parties, look upon the Secretary of State in his new role as house leader as virtually an affront to the opposition. In case after case in the last parliament he, by various methods, delayed or elongated certain stages of legislation and so on, so that they would not be completed until, perhaps, a certain day, or so that the government *would be embarrassed by the tremendously long time taken to get needed interim supply through the house or something of that sort. Now the hon. gentleman is in the position of being the one who has been chosen to ask the opposition to co-operate with the government.
This sort of attitude stems, as far as I can determine, from a colossal conceit on the part of the party now in power. It is a most unfortunate situation for us in this parliament to face at the beginning of a new session. In this connection, certain parties in this house may be under a disadvantage. I say this in no critical way, but two of the parties in this house have never had responsibilities of office. They are, therefore, perhaps not fully aware of the pressures and responsibilities and obligations which a party in power has to support and carry out on behalf of all the Canadian people. I say this in no critical sense, but it is something fully appreciated only by those who have been in that position.
On the other hand, I am a member of a party which, I believe, as a party feels it has no God-given right to be in power all the time. It assumes that the duty of an opposition is an honourable one and that it is not only good for a party to be in office on occasions but that it is good for a party to have experience in opposition from time to
Interim Supply
time. Of course, it is bad for a party to be in opposition indefinitely, and even worse for it to be indefinitely in power.
We suffer from another difficulty, or did in the last parliament, and it is this. I do not think this is representative of the Liberal party as a whole but only of a small group, a sort of syndicate who look upon themselves as having almost a divine right to rule, and when they find themselves in opposition are so astonished by this turn of events that they begin to think that God is no longer in his heavens, and that something has gone wrong. Therefore their objective is to get back into power by any means available to them.
A party in opposition has responsibilities. It has responsibilities not to set precedents which will hamstring parliament for years ahead. A number of very unfortunate precedents were created in the last parliament. For instance, we had the example of this committee spending, speaking from memory, seven days on a 30-day interim supply motion. At this time the present government is asking, and properly so, for four months supply: two months retroactive, as it were, to regularize the spending of moneys provided by Governor General's warrants, and two months in advance. By this reasoning this debate would at the very least be a 14-day debate. If the Minister of Finance were bold enough to suggest, say, on the thirteenth day, that we had talked on this matter long enough, you would have the house leader in the position where, if he were to be consistent, he would have to leap to his feet and scream: "Closure. You cannot do this. You are curtailing the rights of the opposition to speak", and that sort of thing.
Mr. Chairman, there are a number of things which make me wonder, but what makes me wonder most is why the Prime Minister chose this particular colleague of his to fill this role. I think he could have chosen others of his colleagues who would be much more acceptable to the opposition and to the house generally when it comes to asking the house to co-operate and to save time, and to expedite the business of the house, as the house leader must do on occasion. The house leader himself took great exception when the previous house leader suggested that he thought enough time had been spent on any particular aspect of any particular measure, and the only reason I can see for his appointment is that the Prime Minister, because of his associations over a long period of time, finds himself in a situation where he is blinded to these difficulties-and very real difficulties they are. After all, if you look back you will find that at one time the present Secretary of State was in the prime minister's office. The present Prime Minister was

Interim Supply
found a safe seat and brought into parliament as a member of the government. There he established himself with a very excellent record as secretary of state for external affairs. Then you had the opposite event taking place, where the Secretary of State was secretary of the privy council at that time and was found a safe seat in another part of the country and brought into parliament as a cabinet minister.
The operation of this syndicate has continued over the years and is still continuing, because we have further examples of this sort of thing. I could refer to the case of the President of the Privy Council, for example, who came from the office of the then leader of the opposition, although it is immaterial whether he was performing that function or that of the prime minister. The Minister of Labour is in a somewhat different position because he already represented a constituency in this house, and went back to it and won it, which is to his credit. But he spent a period in his leader's office, which is the thing that gives him the key to progress and success, almost a guarantee of inclusion in the cabinet. At some time in some mysterious way he became a member of the syndicate.
"The Establishment".

It is suggested that he became a member of "The Establishment". I had intentionally avoided the use of that word in case it might be interpreted that I was poking fun at my good friend the Secretary of State in comparing him with one of the characters in that skit, and I am not.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is all right; I did not see it.

Hon. members who are new to this house may think that I am very sensitive and have a special revulsion toward this sort of situation, but that is not the case at all. I have been told that in the middle ages, when a victim was thrown into a dungeon, as the situation got worse and worse and the putrefaction increased the prisoner would be completely unaware of the atmosphere in which he was condemned to live, and that it was typical of these prisoners that they could never understand why anyone approaching that atmosphere would be nauseated. Perhaps this is the unfortunate position in which the Prime Minister finds himself, that he is completely unconscious of the atmosphere in which he operates at the moment.
Mr. Chairman, I feel, like the hon. member for Lethbridge, that the original procedure for dealing with interim supply, although the debate being carried on at this time is completely within the rules, has not been an

efficient way for parliament to carry on. I think the committee on rules, if it is set up, should give its attention to this matter. Most committees on rules try to do a good job, but frequently they cannot foresee a mind which operates like that of the Secretary of State, which is able to see all the loopholes whereby a perfectly good rule with a perfectly good intention behind it could be sort of prostituted to party purposes, as was so blatantly done in the last parliament by repeated long debates on interim supply.
I suggest that consideration should be given by the rules committee to the setting up of rules so that if the government introduced the estimates early enough and tabled them, and guaranteed a given number of days, perhaps 35, say, as a minimum-this is something which could be negotiated-and arrangements were made for time to be allotted to every department, and this was completed before the fiscal year commenced, then the supply bill could be passed on the last day before the fiscal year without any further debate. This would eliminate completely the necessity for interim supply.
Interim supply is a fruitless operation in a sense, because we have to go over the ground again when the main estimates are before the committee. No progress is made and no ground is gained; we just ensure by this operation that the civil servants of Canada, the armed forces and we ourselves will be paid. This is the main purpose of it.
The members of the three opposition parties, I think, have at least one common denominator. It is this, that we perhaps take the philosophical view of Kant, that a thing is either intrinsically right or it is intrinsically wrong; that the results that may accrue to the perpetrator of the thing have no bearing on whether it is right or wrong. We, in this party, feel it is wrong to misuse and abuse the rules, even if you are technically within them. We feel that deceit is a wrong thing for a member of parliament to carry out, regardless of what its political results may be. We feel that, therefore, there are certain things which responsible members of parliament should refrain from doing, even if it would be to their political advantage to do them. I do not believe that is too high a moral standard for the Canadian people to expect of their representatives.
However, regretfully, I find that in some segments of the Liberal party there is a very flexible conscience so far as this sort of thing is concerned. It stems, I think, from their overwhelming conceit, their colossal conceit, that they have some divine right to rule, and that if they are not in power Providence made a mistake, which they have to rectify

by hook or by crook. As an example of this sort of thing I recall that last winter, I think it was on December 5 as a matter of fact, in the course of the debate on the Atlantic provinces development board the Secretary of State referred to unemployment insurance for fishermen. I was sitting here at the time and I heard his remarks. He said that some people were under the apprehension that there was, in the minds of some hon. gentlemen on the government side, the notion that it should be scrapped. He was referring to unemployment insurance for fishermen.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Is it not true that a committee appointed by the government to which the hon. gentleman belonged, recommended precisely that, and was that not a logical ground for that statement?

No, I do not consider it was, and for two reasons. First, this was a commission making recommendations and, second, what they did recommend was that a form of unemployment insurance for fishermen should be administered by the Department of Fisheries.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am sure the hon. gentleman, himself, does not want to misrepresent the facts. The Gill committee, and he can read the report, recommended that fishermen be taken off unemployment insurance and some other scheme altogether, not unemployment insurance, be provided instead. This was precisely what I was objecting to, and what I still object to. If that is deceit, it is a very curious definition of deceit.

Well, I think it is definitely deceit for two reasons: One is that there was no definition, it was not even worked out, what this other scheme should be. Second, the recommendation of any commission is not government policy. Surely, the present government is not going to throw the recommendations of the commission in the wastebasket. It would be just as logical for me to say now that the present government is going to scrap unemployment insurance for fishermen.
I wondered why this remark was passed in the house, Mr. Chairman. It is a curious thing, but in parts of the country people can be led to believe that anything that is said in the House of Commons is a fact; that is what is going to happen. Hon. members seem to be regarded as oracles. When an hon. member predicts something is going to happen, that is what is going to happen.
Interim Supply
People believe that Hansard gives it some sanctity, and the program becomes definite.
I found as a fact that in almost every fishing area in the Atlantic provinces it was being said that if the Conservative government were returned to power there would be no unemployment insurance for fishermen. I found that this was an organized stratagem. I found that somebody, presumably from party headquarters, was going back to this statement in Hansard and quoting it as an authority, much in the manner of a dog going back to his vomit. This, Mr. Chairman, is contemptible. I have the highest regard for Canadian citizens and for parliament. I think that anyone or any party who cannot find a better reason than that for trying to persuade people to vote for them is rather barren of a forward looking program.
I have some few questions that I should like to ask the Minister of Finance, but I will dispense with them at the present time. I will refer to them on some later occasion. I do want to return to my original topic. If the Prime Minister actually wants this House of Commons to expedite business, then he should recognize the reasonable demands of the opposition; he should take some cognizance of the natural feelings of hon. members who served in the government and in the opposition during the last parliament. I suggest there are hon. members on the treasury benches who would be more acceptable in this particular role. I throw this suggestion out to the Prime Minister in all seriousness because, after all we could very easily, with aggravation, be tempted to revert to the position the official opposition took in the last parliament. We could spend seven days on a bill for one month's interim supply. I do not believe this sort of thing is good for the country. I do not believe it was good for the country then. I believe the trained observers in the press gallery will recognize this, although some newspapers across Canada have been saying that this is the magic time for parliament to reform. Parliament should not indulge in these tactics any longer. Although, for some mysterious reason, they were all right last year, they are not desirable this year. Now, the logic of that I cannot follow. If the misuse of the rules of parliament in a given way is not wrong for the country in one year, then it is not going to be wrong for the country in the next year.
I should like to point out to you, Mr. Chairman, that the one thing that is saving the country from this sort of situation in the House of Commons, where the desire of certain groups might be to delay and frustrate the progress of parliament, is the sense of responsibility of the present opposition.

Interim Supply

Mr. Chairman, I have no desire to hold up passage of interim supply but I do think the committee is entitled to some statement from the Minister of Justice regarding some of the matters raised by two of my colleagues, the hon. member for Winnipeg North and the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, with reference to the activities of the intelligence and security branch of the R.C.M.P. We regret taking up the time of the committee on this matter, although we are quite within our rights in doing so. But I would point out that on the 17th of May, the day after the house opened,
I put a question to the Minister of Justice asking him if, in view of the discussions that were held in the previous parliament, in view of the article which appeared in Maclean's magazine and in view of the very sweeping statements made by Commissioner Harvison of the R.C.M.P., he would facilitate the setting up of a special committee to look into the activities of the intelligence and security branch of the R.C.M.P. His argument as stated was very brief. He said:
So far as I am concerned, I must tell my hon. friend that at this time I am not disposed to recommend to the house the establishment of such a committee to look into the functions of the branch to which he has referred.
The minister, who is not disposed to recommend the setting up of such a committee, certainly has a duty to come before this committee and before parliament and give some accounting to parliament of the activities of the intelligence and security branch of the R.C.M.P. No one quarrels with the statement made by the hon. member for Bow River who says that the R.C.M.P. is a very fine police force. Of course it is. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police have earned a reputation for efficiency and integrity of which every Canadian is proud.
There are times when, through no fault of their own, they have been used for strikebreaking and there are instances in our past history that no one wants to recall. But that is not the fault of the R.C.M.P., it is the fault of the civil authorities in the use they made of them. We are not quarrelling with the R.C.M.P. We are quarrelling with a branch that has been set up whose activities have in many instances been a threat to civil liberty in this country.
The hon. member for Bow River said that it is the duty of the police to search out communists in political organizations or any other kind of organizations, universities, schools or anywhere else. I am not sure that is a func-

tion of the police. The communist party is not an illegal organization in this country.
I have spent most of my adult life fighting against the communist party and the communist ideology because I agree neither with their political viewpoint nor with their basic philosophy. But in this country there is no law barring people from preaching communism or belonging to the communist party any more than to any other political party. What the police have a responsibility for doing is to seek out those who are guilty of subversion, those who are conspiring to overthrow the government by the use of violence or force, those who are guilty of treason or those who are seeking to betray secrets that will threaten the security of this country. No one questions their right to do that.
What we are questioning is the investigation into organizations which are legitimate organizations and which are protesting, to the best of their understanding and knowledge, against certain public policies. When one sees investigations into the voice of women, into the campaign for nuclear disarmament, into the Canadian peace research institute, this surely is far beyond the responsibility of the R.C.M.P. In many of these instances the claim is that the police have acted rather indiscreetly, but still the practice goes on. I should like to deal with a few of the cases but-

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I wonder whether the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam would permit me to interrupt him. It is almost five o'clock and we were rather hopeful that there might be a possibility of getting the resolution through. I would not ask to have the bill proceeded with. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre said something about last December. Last October the combined opposition in the house gave the government the eighth month of interim supply in one day without a single item of the main estimate having been passed.
