subtopic: ISSUE OF LICENCES SUBJECT TO COMPLIANCE WITH BILL OF RIGHTS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-4, to amend the Broadcasting Act (human rights abuses remedied).
He said: Mr. Speaker, in introducing this bill again I consider I am once more striking a blow for freedom. While members of this group have a definite economic philosophy of life and social philosophy of life, we believe in preserving the rights of the individual in every aspect and sphere of his activities. It is on that account I again introduce this bill.
I am not going to talk at length, because when speaking on the bill on March 16, 1962, I fully outlined the circumstances surrounding it, and anyone who is interested in the detailed history of the background of the bill will find what I have to say, recorded on page 1900 of Hansard for that date.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the first time I had occasion to raise this question in the house was on November 18, 1960. I did so as the result of a conversation I had held with the editor of a local weekly newspaper in my district, with respect to his being denied the right to advertise on the local radio station. Then I discussed the matter with other businessmen in the town of Nelson, and they were most indignant about what they considered this transgression of the bill of rights and the rights of the individual.
As a result of those discussions I agreed to discuss the matter with various legal gentlemen, and finally I discussed it with the learned counsel who advises members of parliament with respect to private bills and other matters. Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, I discussed this question with the chairman of the board of broadcast governors, with officials of the C.B.C. and with the minister of justice, who had the matter investigated and later informed me that he did not consider he would take any action on the legislation under which this type of complaint would be lodged.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the weekly newspaper editor in question had been advertising the date of the issue of his weekly paper, and giving some details as to the leading articles, and so forth, on station CKLN, which is licensed under the authority of the Broadcasting Act. Suddenly he was denied this right by the manager of the station, and I will just read the letter in question:

Broadcasting Act
Mr. M. Carlton 490 Baker Street Nelson, B.C.
Dear Mr. Carlton:
We seem to be on the horns of a dilemma these days, a dilemma which must be obvious to everyone. Now that your paper is establishing itself as a regular advertising media, seeking its business from the same customers as ourselves, it is not reasonable that we should be defeating ourselves by building up in any way the success of a business competitor. We therefore, are invoking section 7 of our contract. As of today's date we are serving you with ten days notice of cancellation of your advertising contract No. 726. I would further bring to your attention items 4 and 6 of the conditions of contract.
Yours sincerely,
A. R. Ramsden, Manager
This weekly newspaper was obtaining advertising that in some cases might have gone to the local radio station, but it was obtaining a greater amount of advertising that would have gone to the Nelson Daily News, and they denied the editor of this weekly paper the right to advertise on this station because he was a competitor. I think those are very unsound grounds indeed, and so did many other business people in the community, and other persons. It is for that reason I enter this bill again this session.
I might explain the weekly newspaper has gone out of business. I might also explain it contained material I was not particularly interested in, and in many cases strongly disagreed with; but that is not my business. That is the business of the public, to refuse to buy something they do not appreciate; but it is my business to protest as a member of parliament, and particularly as a member of this group which never wishes to deny free speech or anything of that sort to anyone.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to quote briefly from the explanatory note in connection with the bill, because it is a rather unusual bill to meet unusual circumstances. I have introduced this bill to provide that a licence to a radio broadcasting station is conditional upon observation of the Canadian Bill of Rights. The explanatory notes read:
Both the English common law and the French civil law recognize the doctrine that the right of the businessman or industrialist to do business only with persons of his choice is subject to restrictions based on reasons of good morals or public order: such is the case where the state takes exclusive control of a commercial field and grants a special privilege or licence in that field to the businessman or industrialist to sell, under monopoly or quasi-monopoly, to the public; the licensee then assumes definite obligations, including the obligation to sell to anyone who is ready to pay the regular price.
Those are quotations from various decisions of the supreme court.
The Canadian parliament, for public convenience, interest and necessity, has by the Radio Act

allowed the crown to grant monopolies by licence to individuals and corporations to operate broadcasting stations for private gain. Under the common law and civil law, therefore, such stations must sell advertising time without discrimination. In 1960, parliament confirmed this law by statute. Section 2 of the Canadian Bill of Rights applies to provide that the Radio Act and the Broadcasting Act shall not be so used as to violate the rights or freedoms of any citizen: e.g., freedom of speech or freedom of press. Presumably, the governor in council might make regulations to control such excesses or the Minister of Transport arbitrarily remedy violations by revocation or suspension of licence. However, for the semblance of impartiality, the seemly method is that parliament decree the means and manner of enforcement. This bill, therefore, so provides.
Clause 1: For clarity, and emphasis of notice to the licensee, this clause provides, generally, that a licence is conditional upon observance of the Canadian Bill of Rights; and, specifically, that there shall be no discrimination by a licensee in providing commercial services to competitor applicants- e.g., freedom of the press includes liberty of circulation and distribution, as well as publication-
-and liberty of circulation and distribution includes the right to compete for advertising space on a government-licensed advertising media -without discrimination because the applicant competes in the newspaper field with the broadcasting monopolist.
I think that is a very sound principle. I continue:
Subsection 6(a) (i) is an adaptation of provincial public utility anti-discrimination law. Subsection (6) (b) follows the procedure in section 3 of the Canadian Bill of Rights in appointing the Minister of Justice to be the deputy of parliament to determine whether a licensee has violated the Canadian Bill of Rights. Upon a violation, the Minister of Transport revokes the licence. The licensee has a right of appeal on any question of law to the exchequer court which may suspend the revocation until the appeal is determined.
Mr. Speaker, I have explained the reason for the introduction of the bill, the purpose of the bill. It is, that after lengthy discussions with persons well informed in the law it was decided that I should introduce this bill to amend the Broadcasting Act, the subtitle of which is "human rights abuses remedied." I want to say, in fairness, that I think this action on the part of the manager of the station was impulsive, because he is a very nice person; so is the editor of the local paper. I am quite sure they regret having taken this action at the time. The paper in question, the competitor, has now ceased to exist but the principle is still followed. It is to make certain that no one will be denied their rights in this way in the future that I introduce this bill and urge the support of hon. members of the house.
Now for the principle of the bill. If any hon. members believe they can suggest an improved bill or amendments to the bill which will make it more effective, I shall be only too pleased to listen. I think we are

on very sound ground in protecting the rights of the individual in this field by the introduction of this bill.

subtopic: ISSUE OF LICENCES SUBJECT TO COMPLIANCE WITH BILL OF RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking to the bill introduced by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) I want to compliment him on his interest in this one individual who was running this paper which has now gone bankrupt. There is from time to time in this house a suggestion that we should have an ombudsman. I suggest that if members of parliament were doing their jobs we would not need an ombudsman, because where small people have been hurt by government or by regulation, members of parliament in doing their job can correct such injustices.
As the hon. member has said, and as the record in previous Hansards will show, the Kootenay Graphic News, which was located in his riding and was a small weekly paper, started up as a very vigorous little paper. This paper endeavoured to obtain and was obtaining advertising on radio station CKLN in Nelson. This station, as the record will show-this is for the benefit of new members-is owned by the News Publishing Co. Ltd., which also owns the Nelson Daily News, as the hon. member pointed out. These two news media, radio station CKLN and the Nelson Daily News, are in effect owned and managed by the same company and the same people. They disliked the thought of the competing newspaper, the Kootenay Graphic News, advertising on the air waves of their radio station and, as the hon. member pointed out, they cancelled his advertising contract. I had hoped that the advertising and the publicity the hon. member's actions would create on behalf of the Kootenay Graphic News would have meant that they would be doing better than if they had continued getting the radio advertising. I am very sorry to hear today that the paper has gone out of business. This is somewhat tragic. I thought that possibly the action of the hon. member in this house and in his constituency would have resulted in the paper doing even better.
In speaking to this bill, Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out three criticisms of it. I have first a general criticism, arising from remedies often suggested by hon. members of the party to which the hon. member belongs. They will see an injustice, a social ill, a wrong, and they will suggest a remedy, the remedy often being worse than the wrong. In certain respects this bill is in that class. I am sure the hon. member for Kootenay West feels he is making a fight on behalf of the little man fighting the big man, and I always admire anyone who is prepared to do this. I think that in protecting the rights of
Broadcasting Act
the little man against the big man we must be very careful that we are not depriving anyone of his proper rights, his due process of law, to which surely he is entitled whether he be a big man or a little man.
I should like to read to the house and put on the record section 6 (a) (i) of this bill:
-will not-
That is, the licensee, the person holding the licence from the government, the radio station:
-will not discriminate or delay, upon reasonable notice given, in furnishing suitable commercial service of the type furnished by the licensee, to any person who may apply therefor and be reasonably entitled thereto and to whom such service reasonably can be supplied by the licensee, for reason only that the person so applying carries on a business that competes with a business in which the licensee has an interest:
With regard to the last part of that clause, which reads, "for reason only that the person so applying carries on a business that competes with a business in which the licensee has an interest", the hon. member for Kootenay West is concerned about a newspaper which is endeavouring to advertise on a radio station. The wording of that clause would also apply to a radio station endeavouring to obtain advertising on a competing radio station. It would seem that under the wording of the bill the competing radio station would be entitled to demand advertising time on his competitor's station. I am not convinced that this would be a particularly healthy situation in the broadcasting business. I am not convinced that it would contribute at all to the health of our broadcasting industry. I am not convinced that it would contribute to the raising of the standards of radio broadcasting across the country.
I would agree with the hon. member that a newspaper, no matter by whom it is owned, should be entitled to advertise on a radio station, and similarly that a radio station should be entitled to advertise in a newspaper. But I am not convinced yet-and the hon. member for Kootenay West is going to have to convince me-that it would be healthy for the broadcasting industry, from the point of view of the public, to allow one radio station to advertise on another. But, more particularly, there is in this bill provision for the Minister of Justice to examine the situation and make a report to the Minister of Transport, and then the Minister of Transport has power to revoke the licence.
I suggest that unless the bill is a little more carefully worded than it is at present, we could have the situation where a competitive radio station in one district would apply for advertising on another station in that district, and if that were refused they could endeavour to have their competitor's licence revoked.

Broadcasting Act
In my city we have at the moment a very competitive radio station and I would think that unless this bill is carefully re-worded, these radio stations, some of which at the moment are not doing too well, would use every etfort to see that the licences of competitors were revoked, not to protect any human rights which had been taken away but simply in an effort to get competitors out of business. I think that is the real danger attaching to this bill and one which should be corrected by redrafting.
In the second place, and this is to me a very serious matter, I feel that the difficulty about solutions recommended by the New Democratic party is that they are so often worse than the problems they are trying to solve. In this bill there is no provision made for a licensee to appeal. Surely, the owner of a radio licence, whether he is big or small, should be entitled to notice, entitled to an appeal and entitled to a hearing. It is elementary justice that such a man should be entitled, before he loses his licence, to make representations to the Minister of Justice or to the Minister of Transport or whoever has power to revoke it. Surely he is entitled to receive notice that his licence may be revoked and to explain, if he wishes, why he took certain action, in the hope that his licence will not in fact be taken away. This is an elementary right which every Canadian should have. Here the only rights the licensee has are set out in subsection (6) (b), and really they provide no rights at all. It says:
The Minister of Justice shall, upon any complaint thereof, ascertain whether a licensee has breached in any particular the condition set out in paragraph (a) and he shall report thereon to the Minister of Transport forthwith and to the House of Commons at the first convenient opportunity.
Nowhere in that procedure is a right given for the licensee who is in danger of losing his licence to be heard. I think that is the real flaw in this bill. Later in the measure it is provided that a licensee who has had his licence revoked may go to the exchequer court and have the matter inquired into. But surely it is not fair to give him rights only after he has lost his licence. Surely we should not put a licensee into a position where only after losing his licence can he resort to this procedure. If, for some reason, he was entitled to refuse advertising, surely we are not going to force him to hire lawyers and follow the complicated procedure of appearing before the exchequer court to have his case heard. It would be much better, I think all hon. members would agree, to allow him to make representations either to the

Minister of Justice or to the Minister of Transport before the licence is lost.
A third matter concerns the way the bill is worded. It is my contention that there is far too much discretion given to the ministers involved. I have great confidence in the ministers of this government and I think we are entitled to have a good deal of confidence in the administrative ability of most ministers, but I think the house should be most careful regarding the discretionary powers it gives to ministers. There are some situations in which this is the only way to deal with some governmental or administrative problem, but I think members of parliament should always be on guard to see that these discretionary powers are kept to a minimum, and where such power is granted it should be spelled out very carefully and the area in which such discretion can be exercised should be clearly defined.
The present bill uses the words "the licensee. . .will not discriminate or delay, upon reasonable notice given-". Surely, it would not be difficult to spell out in the legislation what "reasonable notice" is, whether it be two days, or eight days, or eight weeks. Later on, the text uses the words "in furnishing suitable commercial service" and so on. I have no idea what "suitable commercial service" might be. Further on appears the phrase "to any person who may apply therefor and be reasonably entitled thereto". Surely it would be possible to establish by legislation who is entitled to advertise, because who is to be the judge of whether a man is reasonably entitled to advertise or not? I believe the bill should spell out the right of access to this radio time. Another phrase which occurs in the bill is "to whom such service reasonably can be supplied". This again, is a loose phrase which is bound to give rise to difficulty of interpretation.
All this creates a dangerous situation and one which we must watch, because in this clause we would be giving a minister the power to deprive someone of a licence-a licence which has probably cost him, or the shareholders in the enterprise, a great deal of money. Presumably, too, the station is supplying a service needed by the community to which it is broadcasting; if it is not doing so there are ways of remedying the situation. But we are giving the minister power to take this licence away under a loosely worded statute and we are creating a situation where it would be difficult to argue whether or not a minister had acted rightly in doing so, because of this same looseness of phraseology.
The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) is to be complimented on the vigour with which he has raised this question and endeavoured to protect the rights of the owner

and editor of the Kootenay Graphic News, but in making one correction for the editor [DOT]of that newspaper he is asking us in this particular piece of legislation to take away the rights of others by creating a situation where ministerial discretion could be exercised under the terms of a very loosely worded statute, and then by denying a licensee the right to appeal.
I assume this has not occurred to the hon. member, but his bill would also give rise to a situation which might create havoc in the radio business, inasmuch as it could lead to one radio station advertising on another. I know the hon. member is concerned with a newspaper advertising on a radio station, but I think the situation I have mentioned is one we should bear in mind. As I said at the outset, I believe that a newspaper should certainly have the right to advertise on radio, if it has not already. It would seem to me that to refuse this right of advertising is an action in restraint of trade and should be so declared.
I would think that the hon. member's correct course of action, rather than try to change the Broadcasting Act which deals only with radio, is to endeavour to change the Combines Investigation Act to provide that newspapers can advertise on the radio and that radio stations can advertise in newspapers, regardless of who the owners might be and whether or not they are the same, so that they may advertise in either media.

subtopic: ISSUE OF LICENCES SUBJECT TO COMPLIANCE WITH BILL OF RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to support my hon. friend, the last speaker, in his view that while there may appear to be some individual wrongs to be righted, rather than a collective wrong, the bill in its essence is really determining private rights between two individuals, either corporate or sole. There is very little here of a public nature. It is an attempt, which possibly our friends in the New Democratic party lean to-we all have our faults and this is possibly their fault-to try to interfere with the course of conduct of human beings; to try to over-regulate, to over-legis-late, and to determine how everyone shall act at any given moment. This is probably the great danger of socialism in all its aspects and thinking-that there will be over-regulation and a concomitant loss of individual freedoms. Here we are dealing essentially with a business relationship between two parties.
Mr. Speaker, our friends in the New Democratic party love to put themselves up as the champions of the little man and as defenders of the little man. I think it can be said that we on this side have found there
Broadcasting Act
are no little men but that all Canadian citizens are big men of equal stature; that their rights must be determined by law and that there is not one set of laws or regulations for the little man and another for the big. Every individual is capable of doing some things in a better fashion than others, but the Almighty in some way evens things up and enables us all to do something well. In my humble circumstances my wife is a lot better carpenter than I, and this is one instance of how these things even up. When work is to be done on our storm windows or our kitchen cupboards she does it, because I am not very good with my hands. That is why I say that there are no little men or big men, that each of us can do something better than others, no matter how humble the circumstances. I suggest that the importance of legislation is not to distinguish or to take sides between the little man and the big man, but to make sure that all are equal before the law and that equal justice is done, irrespective of whether we think people are little or big.
This bill tries to do two things, I suggest. When we read the explanatory notes of the bill we find an attempt to interfere in private lives of individual citizens either corporate or sole. It concerns a business matter. In order to try to present this individual business problem which exists between two of his constituents, my hon. friend from Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), in his attempt to right what he feels is an economic wrong-I do not question his motives; I know he is trying to right what he feels is a wrong and is trying hard to draw the bill in such a way as to make it a popular one-has dressed the bill in the very lofty garb of the bill of rights. I suggest, with respect, that if we take a lady of the street and dress her in a Schiaparelli gown, the Schiaparelli gown does not change in any way what is inside the dress. In order to dress this economic problem between two constituents in an attractive garb, the hon. member has brought in the bill of rights. I fail to see, with respect, what the bill of rights has to do with this question in any way, shape or form. For some reason or other the hon. member for Kootenay West, in his explanatory notes, cites the bill of rights of William and Mary, 1688. Whether he does not recognize the more recent bill of rights propounded by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) I do not know. He appears to go back 300 years rather than accept anything which was conceived or concocted by the Leader of the Opposition, and in this he might get considerable support from this side of the house.

Broadcasting Act
In the bill of rights as presently constituted in the 1960 Statutes of Canada, it is quite conceivable that this situation in its loftier aspects is already covered. I do not think there is any hon. member of this house who would oppose any bill which was conceived on the premise that there should be no discrimination in the use of a public licence when it came to race, religion, colour, or such essential freedoms inherent in the bill of rights. But this other economic aspect is a fish of a different fry. I suggest the question of discrimination on proper grounds, such as race, colour or creed, is already dealt with in the bill of rights. I quote from section 2 of the bill of rights:
Every law of Canada shall, unless It is expressly declared by an act of the parliament of Canada that it shall operate notwithstanding the Canadian Bill of Rights be so construed and applied as not to abrogate, abridge or infringe or to authorize the abrogation, abridgment or infringement of any of the rights or freedoms herein recognized and declared, and in particular, no law of Canada shall be construed or applied so as to
(a) authorize or effect the arbitrary detentionet cetera. I will not take up the time of the house by reading the whole section.
Mr. Speaker, I now refer to the definition section in Part II. Section 5(2) says:
The expression "law of Canada" in Part I means an act of the parliament of Canada enacted before or after the coming into force of this act, any order, rule or regulation thereunder, and any law in force in Canada or in any part of Canada at the commencement of this act that is subject to be repealed, abolished or altered by the parliament of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that from reading sections 2 and 5 of the bill of rights together, a licence granted under the statute passed by this house, or a regulation under such statute, is clearly within the bill of rights; so that if, shall we say, someone was refused radio time on the ground that he was a coloured person, or on the ground of his religion not meeting with the approval of the owner of the radio station, the proper legal proceedings could be taken by mandamus, certiorari, prohibition, or under a petition of right to force that owner to grant permission for the use of radio time, under the bill of rights as it now exists. No legislation whatever is needed; we already have it. We have the appropriate remedy to enforce those rights that are given to a person under the bill of rights. With the greatest respect therefore, Mr. Speaker, I submit that the application of the bill of rights to this particular economic problem is just window dressing and has no applicability to the real wrong the hon. member seeks to remedy. It is purely an economic wrong.
Having cleared the air of some of the window dressing concerning the bill of rights,

Mr. Speaker, we approach the question of the right of a newspaper to advertise on a radio station owned by a rival newspaper. This is really the essence of this bill. I concur most wholeheartedly with the hon. member for Kootenay West in his indignation that any licensee should be able to hold a licence to protect his own position and deny other persons the use of a station which is held under a licence from the people of Canada. I may say that, along with the hon. member who spoke before me, some of the provisions of the bill itself disturb me somewhat. Generally speaking the authority in the bill, without taking the time of the house to actually read the clauses, is that any person will be permitted to use the station who may be reasonably entitled so to do. Alternatively, the licence may be arbitrarily cancelled by the Minister of Justice.
I believe the key words of this bill, and I am sure that this is not the intention of the hon. member, are those words, "who may be reasonably entitled thereto". Who decides whether or not he is reasonably entitled to use the station? Actually, it is the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier) who has the discretion to cancel the licence. He has to determine whether or not this person who is seeking cancellation of the licence was reasonably entitled to use the station. These are very arbitrary words, Mr. Speaker. I should like to refer you briefly to the judicial interpretation of this wide discretion contained in the word, "reasonable", to demonstrate to this house that this could give the Minister of Justice unfettered, unlimited, arbitrary and absolute powers over all licensees.
While we know that at the present time this power would not be abused, there might be other individuals at some future date who would abuse such a power. I do not believe this house ever should grant such arbitrary powers to any individual as my hon. friend seeks to do in this bill. On that score, I would refer hon. members to Stroud's judicial dictionary, third edition, at page 2462, where various judicial interpretations of the word, "reasonable" are given. This will indicate the very broad powers which the use of this word would give.
The word "reasonable" has in law the prima facie meaning of "reasonable" in regard to those circumstances of which the actor called on to act reasonably knows or ought to know. However, it would be unreasonable-
This is really the meat of the situation.
-to expect an exact definition of the word reasonable. Reason varies in its conclusions according to the idiosyncracies of the individual-
Again, it is conceivable that we would have a minister of justice in the future whose

idiosyncracies were peculiar; that has happened in the past and it could occur again.
-and the times and circumstances in which he thinks. The reason of other days, with classic logic, sounds now like the jingling of a child's toy. Mankind must be satisfied with the reasonableness within reach, and in a case not covered by authority the verdict of the jury usually determines what is reasonable in each particular case?
In other words, according to the bill the Minister of Justice would, in each case, determine what is reasonable. I think I can cite to my hon. friend the leading authority on the interpretation of this word "reasonable" which I think will shock him to the point where he would be loath to give any one this type of authority. The leading case on the interpretation of the word "reasonable" is the case of Liveridge v. Sir John Anderson, reported in appeal cases, 1942. It is a house of lords decision. Perhaps I should outline to this house very briefly the facts in this case. There was a wartime regulation under which the home secretary could incarcerate someone if he had reasonable grounds to do so. The gist of this case is that the home secretary imprisoned someone and kept him incarcerated for some time. No court, no judicial body, could go behind his actions to see whether or not they were well founded. As long as the home secretary deemed the grounds to be reasonable that was all that mattered.
Well, this bill attempts to give some ex post facto right of appeal. You can appeal after your licence has been cancelled. I think my hon. friend dealt with that aspect of it. However, you could not go behind this decision of the Minister of Justice. If he deemed the grounds reasonable, that would be the end of it. He would have the arbitrary power to withdraw the licence. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this points out the grave danger of trying to legislate perfection into human beings. I think the strength of the party on this side of the house is that we do not expect human beings to be perfect. We do not expect everything to be perfect in this most perfect of all possible worlds. We try to leave as much freedom to the individual as we can to determine his own destiny. At the same time we try, by our legislation, to guarantee that the game will be a fair one and that one person, group or even the government itself, shall not have a great advantage over the individual citizen. When we try to legislate morals and propriety into every aspect of human behaviour, every little corner of business, sometimes we create a wrong that is far greater than the situation we are trying to correct. In this case I suggest that by granting this kind of power to any individual, which could be abused and could create great wrong economically and otherwise if abused,
Broadcasting Act
the wrong we would create would be greater than the good we would do in remedying this individual situation. I think that my friend's desire to remedy this wrong can be met otherwise than by creating this new, pervasive and greater wrong that we would be doing if we gave this kind of power to any minister.

subtopic: ISSUE OF LICENCES SUBJECT TO COMPLIANCE WITH BILL OF RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to say one or two things about the bill and in opening I should like to say to the hon. member who introduced the bill that it is indeed an unfortunate situation that prompted him to do so. On the other hand, I think a word or two should be said about the point that this is not something that is happening to any great extent across Canada. As a matter of fact, I have been told that this is the only case that has been drawn to the attention of the Department of Justice where such a serious violation of what we all consider to be rights has taken place.
I simply want to point out that most of the radio and television stations and other commercial advertising forms with which I have had to deal from time to time have leaned over backwards to try to be fair to all of their advertising accounts. They do this primarily, of course, for the sake of their own public relations, I am sure, and with a view to keeping all of their accounts happy in the future.
In this case I know that the situation was different because the person concerned was dealing with one of his competitors. The hon. member has raised a problem, but I can see some serious weaknesses in the bill from the point of view of actually effecting a solution of it. As has been pointed out by the previous speaker, there is the matter of the words "reasonably entitled" and the interpretation that is going to be placed on them. I know, for example, that a person may be reasonably entitled to something, but then the next matter that may come up is how much is he reasonably entitled to.
If the provisions of this bill were applied and the radio station accepted a very limited amount of advertising at an hour that was inappropriate or not conducive to having a reasonably large audience, the radio station could in fact comply with the regulations anticipated in the bill while at the same time almost denying the account the effectiveness desired from the advertising.
I simply want to say I do not believe this is a common practice. It certainly is not in those areas where I have had contact with radio stations. As the previous speaker pointed out, by passing this legislation we would be imposing more regulations to deal with an isolated problem even though it is a

Broadcasting Act
serious one to the man involved and I do not think we should do so until we And that there are a greater number of violations of human rights. I am sympathetic with regard to the situation which has been raised by the hon. member who introduced the bill. At the same time, since it is not a common thing maybe we should have another look at it.

subtopic: ISSUE OF LICENCES SUBJECT TO COMPLIANCE WITH BILL OF RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this bill came up in an earlier parliament on March 16, 1962, the then member for Lapointe, Mr. Brassard, said, as found on page 1906 of Hansard:
I believe all hon. members are aware of the sense of justice and social sense which characterize the hon. member for Kootenay West, and I am not surprised to hear him take up the defence of anyone who seems to be victimized.
We are not talking out this measure for the sake of talking it out. In spite of the fact that on the facts it would appear that a licensee granted a licence from a federal authority appears to be limiting the service of that right, we earnestly think that there are certain real weaknesses in the bill which we would ask the good member for Kootenay West to consider.
In the first place, the bill by its terms purports to wipe out a vested right granted by licence by means of the exercise of ministerial discretion without a hearing. Under the terms of the bill no hearing is provided as to the facts. As we go on we find there is provision for an appeal to the exchequer court, not as to the facts but on a question of law alone. That means that there is a limited type of appeal. It means that the facts of the case will never have been heard adequately from the standpoint of the licensee.
When we consider the number of limiting and inhibiting factors at the present time which tend to constrict the kind of broadcasting that there is in Canada, we realize that this measure would create a very difficult situation for people in this particular media. On the face of the matter it appears as though there has been an injustice done in this one riding in Canada. I too have tried to make a careful examination of how frequently such a thing has occurred and I am assured by the B.B.G. that this is the only case in all Canada.
The active member for Kootenay West, who so valiantly champions his riding and has done so on many occasions, brought this matter to the attention of the House of Commons on November 18, 1960, by way of a question which was answered by the then minister of national revenue. Then he went on to explore the various possibilities in order to see whether there was any chance

of obtaining any assistance in this particular case under the combines legislation. I think he found it was impossible. When we consider that a broadcaster is being asked under this bill to accept material of his competitor that would in fact worsen his business position, we have to ask the member to consider that what the bill really means is that the C.B.C. could be compelled to advertise programs of the private broadcasters. Do we really want to go that far? Is this what the bill means? We appreciate that there are limitations on private rights, and there must be. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I wonder whether the house leader would indicate to a very co-operative house what the business is for next week?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Nothing would give me greater pleasure than to be able to take at its face value, which of course I do, the suggestion of the hon. gentleman opposite that the house will be co-operative next week. It is in that spirit that I express the hope that we will be able to deal with interim supply with almost as much dispatch as it was dealt with in late September or early October of last year. As soon as that is completed, of course, we will go on with the debate on the committee on defence, and I would also express the hope that that might be disposed of on Monday. After that we will go ahead with the resolution to precede the bill respecting the economic council.
We also hope next week to take the bill respecting the department of industry, the bill respecting the Department of Agriculture and the resolutions preceding them and, if it can be arranged, the resolution and the bill respecting the municipal development and loan board. I wish I could indicate clearly the order in which those measures will be taken but one or two of my colleagues have made certain commitments which force them to be out of Ottawa on public business on one or two days next week, and I regretfully have to admit that this will have to be arranged as the week goes on, but I hope to give as much notice as possible of the order in which these last three measures will be taken. The first three items, barring an act of God, will be interim supply until completed, then the defence committee until it is completed, the resolution stage of the economic council, and we hope to take the bill next day after the resolution.
You would take the bill on that before the next resolution?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
That would depend on the time of day. If we finish the economic council resolution in the middle of the day we cannot take the bill immediately afterwards, under the rules, and we would not ask to have them waived because hon. members should have a chance to read the bill. If the economic
Business of the House council resolution stage finished in the middle of the day, then we would take one of the other resolutions that day, and come back later to the bill. It is a little complicated, but I hope all hon. members understand these matters.
